topic: medieval anchoress living-burial ritual and Julian of Norwich's 20-year enclosure
title: Medieval Women Who Asked The Church To Bury Them Alive
description: The medieval ritual where women asked to be sealed alive in a church wall, and the anchoress who spent 20 years like that and wrote what's considered the earliest surviving English-language book by a woman. AI-narrated commentary on public historical record, written as original commentary.

hook_candidates.text: Medieval women chose to be sealed in their own grave, alive.
Priests really did read a living woman her own funeral rites, then bricked the door shut.
What if the last rites read over you were the start of your life, not the end?
In 1373, a woman named Julian asked her priest to seal her into a stone room forever.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who jokes about wanting to disappear from everyone forever, because a medieval woman actually did it.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume medieval women who were sealed alive in their own grave had no choice in it.
closing_comment: That medieval anchoress, Julian, who asked the church to seal her alive, still out-wrote most of her century from behind three windows.

sources.note: Notre Dame medieval studies blog confirms the enclosure rite borrowed burial liturgy, including a grave dug inside the cell.
Confirms Julian of Norwich's anchorhold had three windows and she remained enclosed roughly 20 years.
Confirms Revelations of Divine Love is the earliest surviving English-language book known written by a woman.

beats.text: Medieval women chose to be sealed in their own **grave**, alive.
beats.broll_query: a small arched stone doorway in a medieval church wall, half bricked shut, faint candlelight glowing through the remaining gap

beats.text: Her enclosure was treated like a real **funeral**.
beats.broll_query: a medieval woman lying face down before a stone church altar, candles, a solemn priest standing over her

beats.text: Priests read her burial rite, sang the **corpse hymn**, then bricked her door.
beats.broll_query: a stonemason's hands pressing wet mortar and a brick into a small church wall doorway, dusk light

beats.text: At least the wake was well-attended.
beats.broll_query: a small crowd of medieval villagers in wool cloaks standing solemnly outside a church door at dusk, holding candles

beats.text: Her cell had exactly **three** windows, and no door.
beats.broll_query: three narrow stone window slits cut into a thick medieval wall, one sealed doorway beside them, moss in the cracks

beats.text: One faced the altar, one passed food, one let visitors speak.
beats.broll_query: a gloved hand passing a small wooden bowl of bread through a narrow stone window slit into darkness

beats.text: Still more privacy than open-plan offices.
beats.broll_query: a cramped modern open-plan office with grey cubicles and fluorescent lighting, workers hunched at desks

beats.text: One anchoress, Julian, stayed sealed inside for roughly **twenty years**.
beats.broll_query: an aging medieval woman writing by candlelight at a small wooden desk inside a bare stone room, quill in hand

beats.text: She never left again. What she wrote became the **earliest surviving** English book by a woman.
beats.broll_query: a weathered handwritten medieval manuscript page under candlelight, ink quill resting beside faded brown script

beats.text: Historians still debate how strictly every anchoress followed that same rite.
